title: A 1% Fee Quietly Costs You $111,000

beats.say: A one percent fee sounds like nothing. Over thirty years, it can cost about one hundred eleven thousand dollars.
beats.visual: a single drop of water falling into a huge dark pool, extreme close-up

beats.say: This is an illustration, not a promise. We assume ten thousand dollars to start and five hundred dollars a month.
beats.visual: an old brass calculator beside a stack of ledgers under a green banker lamp, no people

beats.say: Picture two investors. Both put in the same money for thirty years.
beats.visual: two identical empty wooden chairs facing a window at dawn, no people

beats.say: The first earns seven percent a year. After thirty years, about six hundred forty three thousand dollars.
beats.visual: a tall golden staircase climbing into soft clouds, wide shot, no people

beats.say: The second pays a one percent fee, so earns six percent. About five hundred thirty two thousand dollars.
beats.visual: a slightly shorter silver staircase climbing into soft clouds, wide shot, no people

beats.say: Same deposits. Same time. One percent apart.
beats.visual: two parallel train tracks leaving a station into misty morning light, no people

beats.say: The gap is about one hundred eleven thousand dollars.
beats.visual: a large stack of gold coins crumbling from one side in a dark room, dramatic light

beats.say: Here is the part nobody tells you. Fees do not send a bill. They just take a little from your growth every single year.
beats.visual: a thin crack slowly spreading across a glass bowl of coins, extreme close-up

beats.say: Over time, the money you never see leave is the money you never get to compound.
beats.visual: a leaking brass tap dripping slowly into an old metal bucket, moody light

beats.say: The honest catch: real returns bounce around, and a pricier fund is sometimes worth it. Your numbers will differ.
beats.visual: a stormy sea with waves rising and falling under a heavy sky and a lighthouse

beats.say: So the move is simple: find the fee on your funds, then compare it.
beats.visual: a hand holding a magnifying glass over an old printed page, close-up, no face

beats.say: A small number checked once can be worth a lot over decades.
beats.visual: a single stone step leading up a long quiet staircase into morning mist, no people

beats.say: Follow for the money rules school never taught you.
beats.visual: an empty highway stretching toward a glowing sunrise horizon, wide shot

description: A one percent fee sounds tiny. On 10,000 dollars plus 500 dollars a month for 30 years at 7 percent versus 6 percent, the gap is about 111,000 dollars. An illustration, not a promise.
first_comment: Do you know the fees on your account? Educational only, not financial advice.

facts.claim: $10,000 start + $6,000/year for 30 years, annual compounding: 7% gives about $642,887; 6% gives about $531,784; gap about $111,103
Fund fees (expense ratios) reduce returns every year
facts.basis: SEC Investor.gov, 'Mutual Fund Fees and Expenses'

facts.claim: Assumed returns are an illustration, not a forecast

caption: $10,000 plus $500 a month for 30 years: 7% grows to about $643K, 6% (a 1% fee) to about $532K. The gap is about $111K. An illustration, not a promise. Educational content, not financial advice.
